ageing_relevance.rationale: Cystatin C is a well-known ageing/mortality biomarker, a GrimAge component, with sizeable ageing literature share and associations with AMD, CKD and cardiovascular disease. It is mainly a biomarker, so causality is uncertain.

evidence.value: One of seven plasma proteins whose DNA-methylation surrogates make up GrimAge

background_knowledge: Circulating cystatin C is used as a kidney function marker and predicts mortality and cardiovascular risk (not from tools).
The DNAm surrogate is a methylation estimate, not measured protein.

mechanism.rationale: Function as a cysteine protease (cathepsin) inhibitor is known, and amyloid-forming variants cause hereditary cerebral haemorrhage. The direction for ageing is unclear: high levels mark risk, but the protein may be protective (anti-protease, anti-amyloid).

evidence.value: As an inhibitor of cysteine proteinases, this protein is thought to serve an important physiological role as a local regulator of this enzyme activity

background_knowledge: Cystatin C reportedly has neuroprotective and anti-amyloid-beta aggregation roles; its plasma level is also affected by GFR, inflammation and smoking.

tractability.rationale: Small-molecule evidence (structure with ligand, high-quality pocket) and antibody feasibility as a secreted protein exist, but there is no clinical-stage precedence. The direction is also unclear, and inhibiting a protease inhibitor is not obviously useful.

safety.rationale: No liabilities are listed, but absence of data is not safety. Its biology (protease inhibition, and amyloid variants causing cerebral haemorrhage) gives some caution for lowering it.
background_knowledge: Lowering a physiological protease inhibitor could unbalance cathepsin activity; this is a theoretical concern.

clinical_precedence.rationale: No drugs have reached the clinic against CST3.

assessment.summary: CST3 (cystatin C) is a secreted cysteine protease inhibitor and a well-established ageing and mortality biomarker. It is one of the GrimAge plasma-protein surrogates, and about 25% of its papers mention ageing. Disease links include AMD, CKD, cardiovascular disease and amyloid angiopathy. It has no clinical candidates and no listed safety liabilities, and it has small-molecule and antibody tractability signals. It is probably a marker rather than a driver, and the direction of modulation is unclear, so I would treat it as a biomarker or pharmacodynamic readout rather than a lead target.
key_uncertainties: Whether CST3 is causal in ageing or only a marker, since levels are confounded by kidney function, inflammation and smoking
Direction of modulation: higher levels mark risk, but the protein may be protective (anti-protease, neuroprotective)
GrimAge surrogate is a DNA-methylation estimate, not measured protein
No clinical precedence and no safety data from modulation
